frames.narration: The product manager says the photo app expects 10 million daily users who upload 2 photos each. Before drawing any boxes, the engineer does a back-of-the-envelope estimate.

The engineer writes down the other assumptions with units: a photo is 500 KB after compression, the peak is 3 times the average, photos are kept for 1 year. Anyone can now change one of them and redo the sum.
How many seconds are in a day? The cheat sheet says 86,400, and to round hard the engineer uses 100,000. Every answer will come out about 14% low, which will not change the design.
Uploads per day: 10 million users times 2 uploads is 20 million, or 2 times 10 to the 7th. Dividing by 10 to the 5th seconds leaves 2 times 10 to the 2nd: about 200 uploads a second on average.
Traffic is not flat: evenings are busier than nights. With a peak of 3 times the average, the system must handle 600 uploads a second, not 200.
Storage: 20 million photos times 500 KB is 10 TB a day. Times 365 days is 3,650 TB, or 3.65 PB, in a year (about 4 PB if 365 is rounded to 400). Three copies for safety would make it around 11 PB.

messages.label: 10 TB a day, 3.65 PB a year

frames.narration: Bandwidth: 600 uploads a second times 500 KB is 300 MB/s. Network links are rated in bits and a byte is 8 bits, so that is 2,400 Mbps, or 2.4 Gbps.

The latency ladder shapes the design: reading from memory is about 100 ns, an SSD about 100 us, a round trip inside one data centre about 0.5 ms and a round trip to another region about 100 ms. So each upload is written to nearby storage first and copied to other regions in the background.

Sanity check: 2.4 Gbps is 24% of one 10 Gbps link, and 600 uploads a second is easily spread over a few servers, so nothing looks absurd. The answer is good enough to choose the design, and the assumptions are ready to be argued with.
